title: Composites and common factors
summary: PLS-SEM represents constructs as weighted composites of their indicators, CB-SEM as common factors behind them; the same diagram therefore has two different estimands.

body.text: A [[common-factor]] model says the indicators share one underlying cause. The construct is what the indicators have in common; whatever is specific to an item is treated as error. A [[composite]] is a weighted sum of the indicators. It contains everything in them, including their measurement error.

body.explanation: A composite C is a weighted sum of its k standardised indicators x with weights w. PLS-SEM estimates the weights; the construct score is then an exact linear combination of observed data.

body.text: [[pls-sem]] estimates composites; [[cb-sem]] estimates common factors. When the constructs really are common factors, classic PLS tends to overestimate loadings and to underestimate the correlations between constructs, because composites still carry measurement error (Dijkstra & Henseler 2015). Paths are biased as a consequence: the main paths are usually too small, but with several correlated predictors an individual path can also come out too large. On the service-quality example the standardised path SAT → LOY is .534 with classic PLS, .602 with consistent PLS and .598 with CB-SEM (ML).

Neither estimand is wrong in general. Composites suit constructs that are designed or defined as combinations, such as an index; common factors suit attributes measured by interchangeable items (Henseler 2017; Rigdon 2012). Choose by your theory of the construct, not by which method gives larger or more significant numbers (Sarstedt et al. 2016).

mistake.title: Comparing PLS and CB numbers as if they estimated the same thing
mistake.text: A PLS path of .53 and a CB path of .60 are not a disagreement to be resolved by picking one: they target different quantities. Report which estimand your method addresses and why.

tryIt.task: Open the service-quality example. Run CB-SEM (ML), then switch the method to PLS-SEM and run again. Compare the standardised path SAT → LOY and the R² of LOY.

checks.question: On the same data the classic PLS path SAT → LOY is .534 and the CB-SEM standardised path is .598. What is the main reason?

options.text: Composites include measurement error, which attenuates relations between them; CB-SEM separates the error.
options.feedback: Correct. With reflective constructs, composite-based paths are typically smaller than factor-based ones.

options.text: PLS-SEM is simply biased and should not be used.
options.feedback: PLS consistently estimates composite-model parameters. It is "biased" only if you use it to estimate a common-factor model, which is what PLSc is for.

options.text: The sample is too small for PLS.
options.feedback: The gap comes from the estimand, not from sample size; it does not disappear in large samples.
The .598 is CB-SEM's standardised estimate, so the scales are comparable; the difference is conceptual.

checks.explanation: Different estimands, not a contest between methods.

checks.question: Managers define "service convenience" as a weighted combination of opening hours, location, online booking and parking. Which representation fits this construct?

options.feedback: Correct. The construct is defined by its components; it is not a common cause of them.
A common factor assumes one cause of all four items, so they should correlate highly. Opening hours and parking need not correlate at all.

options.text: Either, as long as the reliability is high
options.feedback: Reliability is a common-factor concept and is not the right criterion for choosing how to represent an index.

checks.explanation: The construct's definition decides the representation.
